newsitem.title: DUBAI: Mideast Gulf oil outlook - refiners boost profits.
newsitem.headline: Mideast Gulf oil outlook - refiners boost profits.

text.p: State-owned oil refiners in the Middle East Gulf are enjoying one of the most sustained and profitable trading periods since the 1990-1991 Gulf War, trade and refining sources in the region said on Thursday.

Strong crude oil markets have kept Gulf product prices stubbornly close to five-year highs despite middle distillate supply length and muted Indian subcontinent buying which has dampened spot market premiums to independent price quotes.

The estimated 250,000 barrels per day (bpd) of gas oil which is exported from the Gulf to Indian subcontinent, Asian and east African markets was assessed at $29.35 a barrel fob Gulf on Thursday, its highest level since the Gulf War.
But despite the revenue windfall for regional refiners, premiums for trade sellers were being eroded by unsold cargoes still available for end November and December loading.

"There are 10 to 12 cargoes available...there are large volumes uncommitted," said one trader who assessed one percent sulphur gas oil at a 55 cents quote premium and 85 cents for 0.5 percent quality material.
Gas oil cargoes have traded in recent months above a $1 premium but a downturn in key Indian subcontinent and east African buying has trimmed premiums back.
Indian Oil Corp's (IOC) next gas oil buying tender will close November 20-21 for January delivery. The state firm bought 520,000 of gas oil tonnes in its latest tender for December.
Jet fuel markets have also struggled to hold up. Two cargoes sold into Japan at premiums of 50 cents and 60 cents though regular kerosene's premium was talked as firm as $1.00.
An estimated 150,000 bpd of jet and kerosene is exported from the Gulf.

Naphtha markets led the region's oil product bull-run, reversing heavy losses last week to bounce back to five-year highs on the back of strong Asian petrochemical feedstock requirements and tough Saudi term premiums, traders said.
Premiums for naphtha were assessed at $11-12 over independent price quotes, compared to $7-8 at the start of the year and a year-on-year $3-4.
"Aramco's (term) contracts have certainly helped the premiums," one trader said.
Saudi Aramco was able to secure a $6.50 premium for A-180 naphtha deliveries in the first half of 1997, compared to $3.40 in the second half of this year.
Naphtha was assessed at $204 a tonne with supplies tight.
